What is the difference between a region and a zone?

A region is a geographic location (e.g. asia-south1) containing several isolated zones (asia-south1-a/b/c), each an independent failure domain. Zonal resources such as VMs fail with their zone, so for HA you spread instances across zones (regional MIGs, Cloud SQL HA). Regional services like Cloud Run are already replicated across zones.
What is a service account and how should an app authenticate to GCP services?

A service account is a non-human identity for applications. Attach a dedicated SA to the Cloud Run service, VM or GKE workload (via Workload Identity) and grant it only needed roles. Client libraries use Application Default Credentials, fetching short-lived tokens from the metadata server – no key files in code or images. Use Workload Identity Federation for external CI instead of exported JSON keys.
Basic vs predefined vs custom IAM roles?

Basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) apply across all services and are too broad for production. Predefined roles are curated per service by Google, e.g. roles/run.invoker or roles/cloudsql.client. Custom roles bundle exactly the permissions you choose when predefined roles are too wide. Follow least privilege and grant roles to groups or SAs, not individuals.
Cloud Run vs Compute Engine vs GKE vs App Engine – when to choose which?

Cloud Run: stateless containerised HTTP services or jobs, minimal ops, scale to zero – the default for most APIs. GKE: many services needing Kubernetes features (custom networking, sidecars, stateful sets, fine-grained control). Compute Engine: full OS control, legacy or stateful software, special hardware (GPUs). App Engine: legacy PaaS apps; new projects generally use Cloud Run.
What are Cloud Run's requirements and limitations?

The container must listen on the port given by the PORT env var (default 8080), be stateless, and handle requests within the configured timeout (up to 60 minutes). The filesystem is in-memory and ephemeral, instances can be stopped anytime, and with request-based billing CPU is only guaranteed while handling requests (instance-based billing keeps it allocated for background work). Cold starts matter for JVM apps.
💡 Use --min-instances and startup CPU boost for latency-sensitive Spring Boot services.
How do you connect a Cloud Run Spring Boot service to Cloud SQL securely?

Grant the service account roles/cloudsql.client, add the instance with --add-cloudsql-instances and use the Cloud SQL Java connector (socket factory) or Unix socket, which authenticate via IAM and encrypt traffic. Alternatively, use private IP with Direct VPC egress. Store the DB password in Secret Manager or use IAM database authentication to avoid passwords entirely.
How do you store secrets on GCP?

Use Secret Manager: secrets are versioned, encrypted, access-controlled with IAM and audited. Inject them into Cloud Run as env vars or mounted files (--set-secrets), read them with client libraries, or via Spring Cloud GCP. Avoid plain env vars in deploy scripts, secrets in Git, or secrets baked into images.
What is Artifact Registry and how does it relate to Container Registry?

Artifact Registry is GCP's managed repository for container images and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, etc.) with regional repos, IAM and vulnerability scanning. It is the successor to Container Registry (gcr.io), which has been deprecated. Authenticate Docker with gcloud auth configure-docker REGION-docker.pkg.dev.
Explain Cloud Storage classes and how to give users temporary access to a private file.

Standard for frequently accessed data; Nearline, Coldline and Archive for data accessed roughly monthly, quarterly or yearly – cheaper storage but retrieval fees and minimum durations. Lifecycle rules can transition or delete objects. For temporary private access generate a signed URL from the backend with an expiry, so the browser uploads/downloads directly without credentials or making the bucket public.
How would you set up CI/CD for a Spring Boot app on GCP?

Create a Cloud Build trigger on pushes to main that runs tests, builds the image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to Artifact Registry and runs gcloud run deploy. Use a dedicated build service account with minimal roles. For multiple environments use Cloud Deploy or separate triggers, and Cloud Run traffic splitting for canary releases and fast rollback to a previous revision.
How do firewall rules work in a GCP VPC?

Firewall rules are defined at the VPC level, are stateful (return traffic allowed automatically), and target instances by network tag, service account or all instances. Implied rules deny all ingress and allow all egress; you add allow rules such as tcp:443 from 0.0.0.0/0 for web tags, and restrict SSH to IAP's range (35.235.240.0/20) instead of the whole internet.
How do you view logs and set up alerts for a Cloud Run service?

Stdout/stderr go to Cloud Logging automatically; filter in Logs Explorer by resource.type="cloud_run_revision" and severity, ideally using structured JSON logs. In Cloud Monitoring create alerting policies on metrics like 5xx rate, request latency or instance count, or on log-based metrics, and route notifications to email/Slack. Uptime checks catch full outages.
How does Cloud Run scale?

Cloud Run adds instances based on incoming concurrent requests and CPU, up to --max-instances, and scales down to --min-instances (zero by default). Each instance handles up to the configured concurrency (default 80, max 1000). Set max instances to protect downstream resources like the Cloud SQL connection limit, and size the HikariCP pool accordingly.
How would you deploy a PHP application on GCP?

The modern route is to containerise it (e.g. php:8.3-apache or nginx + php-fpm), push to Artifact Registry and deploy on Cloud Run, using Cloud SQL for MySQL and Cloud Storage for uploads since the container filesystem is ephemeral. Alternatively run a LAMP stack on a Compute Engine VM with firewall rules for HTTP/HTTPS and manage patching yourself. App Engine Standard also supports PHP runtimes.
How do you control GCP costs?

Set billing budgets with alerts, label resources by team/environment, and review billing reports (or export to BigQuery). Use scale-to-zero services, right-size VMs and databases (Recommender suggestions), committed-use discounts for steady workloads, Spot VMs for batch, storage lifecycle rules, and delete idle disks, IPs and snapshots. Watch network egress, which is often an overlooked cost.

What is Pub/Sub and how does it compare to Kafka?

Pub/Sub is a fully managed, serverless messaging service: topics, subscriptions (each gets every message), pull or push delivery, at-least-once by default, with dead-letter topics and ordering keys. Kafka is a distributed log you run (or buy managed) with partitions, consumer groups, long retention and replay by offset. Pub/Sub needs no capacity planning and suits event-driven GCP apps; Kafka gives more control over ordering, retention and stream processing. GCP also offers Managed Service for Apache Kafka if you need Kafka APIs.
How do you run scheduled or background jobs on GCP?

For cron, Cloud Scheduler calls an HTTP endpoint, publishes to Pub/Sub or starts a Cloud Run job (a container that runs to completion, with retries and parallel tasks). For per-item async work with rate limiting, enqueue tasks in Cloud Tasks. For reacting to events like a file landing in Cloud Storage, use Eventarc to trigger a Cloud Run service. Avoid long work inside a normal Cloud Run request — requests have a timeout and CPU may be throttled outside requests unless "CPU always allocated" is set.
Cloud SQL vs Firestore vs Spanner vs BigQuery — how do you choose?

Relational, transactional, regional app with JPA → Cloud SQL. Global scale with horizontal writes and strong consistency → Spanner. Document data, mobile/web clients, real-time listeners → Firestore. Analytics over large datasets with SQL → BigQuery (not for OLTP). Add Memorystore for caching. 💡 Start with Cloud SQL for most Spring Boot apps; justify anything else by a specific requirement.
How do you make Cloud SQL highly available and recoverable?

Enable the HA configuration: a synchronous standby in another zone with automatic failover (a short outage of seconds to a minute; apps need connection retry, which HikariCP plus retries handles). Turn on automated backups and point-in-time recovery (binary logs / WAL), test restores regularly, and add read replicas (also cross-region) for read scaling or disaster recovery. Use maintenance windows and deny periods to control upgrades.
How does Cloud Run handle deployments and rollbacks?

Each deploy creates an immutable revision. Traffic can be split between revisions by percentage, so you can canary (--no-traffic deploy, then gcloud run services update-traffic --to-revisions=rev2=10), use tagged revision URLs for testing, and roll back instantly by sending 100% back to the previous revision. Revisions also capture env vars, secrets and scaling settings, so config changes are versioned too.
Explain the GCP resource hierarchy and IAM inheritance.

Organization → folders → projects → resources. IAM policies set at a higher level are inherited by everything below and the effective policy is the union, so a broad grant at the folder level cannot be removed at the project level (deny policies are the exception). Organization Policies add constraints like allowed locations or disabling service-account key creation. Billing is linked at the project level, and projects are the main boundary for isolation between environments.
Why use Terraform for GCP instead of the console or gcloud scripts?

Terraform is declarative: you describe the desired state and it computes a plan of changes, which can be reviewed in a PR and applied by CI. State (stored remotely in a GCS bucket with locking) lets it detect drift and manage dependencies between resources. It makes environments reproducible (dev and prod from the same modules) and auditable. Console clicks are fine for exploration, but not for production infrastructure.
How does a GitHub Actions or Jenkins pipeline deploy to GCP without a service-account key file?

Use Workload Identity Federation: GCP trusts the CI system's OIDC token (for example GitHub's), exchanges it for short-lived credentials, and lets the pipeline impersonate a deploy service account with only the roles it needs (Artifact Registry Writer, Cloud Run Developer, Service Account User). No long-lived JSON key exists to leak or rotate. On GKE, Workload Identity does the same for pods.
Cloud Run service vs Cloud Run job vs Cloud Run functions (Cloud Functions)?

| Service | Job | Functions
You deploy | A container that listens on $PORT | A container that runs and exits | Source code for one function
Started by | HTTP requests (or events via Eventarc) | Manually, Cloud Scheduler or a workflow | HTTP or events
Lifetime | Per request, instances scale to zero | Until the task finishes; can split into parallel tasks | Per invocation
Good for | Spring Boot REST APIs, Angular hosting | Nightly exports, batch imports, migrations | Small glue code, e.g. react to a file upload
Rule of thumb: if something waits for requests, it is a service; if it should finish and stop, it is a job; reach for a function when writing a whole container would be overkill.
Request-based vs instance-based billing on Cloud Run, and min instances 0 vs 1+?

| Request-based (default) | Instance-based
CPU available | Only while handling requests (plus startup and shutdown) | The whole time the instance exists
Background work after the response | Throttled, unreliable | Works (@Async, schedulers, Kafka consumers)
You pay for | Time spent serving requests | Whole instance lifetime
Good for | Spiky, request-only APIs | Steady traffic or background processing
Rule of thumb: min instances 0 is cheapest but gives JVM cold starts; set min instances to 1 or more for user-facing Spring Boot APIs, and use instance-based billing only if the app really works outside requests.
Cloud Logging vs Cloud Monitoring vs Cloud Trace vs Error Reporting?

Service | Answers | Data | Example
Cloud Logging | What happened, in detail? | Log entries (stdout, stderr, audit logs) | Find the log lines for one request ID
Cloud Monitoring | How is it doing over time? | Metrics, uptime checks, alert policies | Alert when p95 latency > 1 s
Cloud Trace | Where did the time go? | Distributed traces and spans | The SQL call that made a request slow
Error Reporting | Which exceptions are new or frequent? | Stack traces found in logs, grouped | A new NullPointerException after a release
Rule of thumb: write structured JSON logs to stdout with a trace ID, and all four tools can link to each other for the same request.
Persistent Disk vs Filestore vs Cloud Storage?

| Persistent Disk | Filestore | Cloud Storage
Type | Block storage | Managed NFS file share | Object storage
Access | Attached to a VM (or GKE node) | Mounted by many clients at once | HTTP API / client libraries from anywhere
Scope | Zonal or regional | Zonal or regional instance | Regional, dual-region or multi-region bucket
Good for | A VM's OS disk, a self-managed database | Legacy apps that need a shared POSIX folder | Uploads, reports, backups, static files
Rule of thumb: for a stateless Spring Boot app, store uploaded documents in Cloud Storage and keep only metadata in Cloud SQL; use disks or Filestore only when software insists on a file system.
